title: Blocking Mobile Internet on Smartphones Improves Sustained Attention, Mental Health, and Subjective Well-Being

source.title: Blocking mobile internet on smartphones improves sustained attention, mental health, and subjective well-being
source.authors: Noah Castelo, Kostadin Kushlev, Adrian F. Ward, Michael Esterman, Peter B. Reiner

studies.title: Month-long crossover waitlist-control RCT blocking mobile internet
studies.description: The paper's single empirical study: a preregistered, two-arm (Intervention / Delayed Intervention), three-wave (T1/T2/T3), crossover RCT in which 467 Prolific-recruited iPhone users had mobile internet access blocked on their smartphone for 2 of the study's 4 weeks.

nodes.title: Public concern about smartphone/internet overuse

fields.label: Reported prevalence of concern
fields.value: Half of American smartphone users, and >80% of users under 30, worry they use their device too much; correlational research links smartphone use to poorer SWB, mental health, and attentional abilities.

nodes.summary: Motivating background: widespread concern about smartphone/mobile-internet overuse and weak prior causal evidence.

nodes.title: Preregistered primary hypothesis

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Blocking mobile internet access on participants' smartphones for 2 weeks will improve subjective well-being (SWB), mental health, and attentional functioning (self-reported attentional awareness and objectively measured sustained attention via gradCPT), relative to a waitlist control.

nodes.summary: The study's three preregistered primary outcomes.

nodes.title: Crossover waitlist-control RCT (3 waves, 2 arms)

fields.label: Design
fields.value: Two-arm randomized, waitlist-controlled crossover design. Intervention group blocks all mobile internet access (Wi-Fi and mobile data) on their smartphone for weeks 1–2 (T1–T2) then regains access for weeks 3–4 (T2–T3). Delayed Intervention group has normal access for weeks 1–2 (control) then blocks mobile internet for weeks 3–4 (T2–T3). All measures taken at T1 (baseline), T2 (+2 weeks), T3 (+4 weeks).

fields.label: Rationale for waitlist (not active) control
fields.value: A waitlist control was chosen intentionally because the primary research goal is to examine the effect of the status quo (constant mobile internet access), not to compare against an alternative active intervention.

fields.label: SMS experience-sampling cadence (implementation choice)
fields.value: The source text gives two different sets of four weekdays for the thrice-weekly... (four times per week) SMS prompts: p.6 and the SI Appendix say Monday/Wednesday/Friday/Sunday, while p.7 and p.9 say Mondays/Wednesdays/Fridays/Saturdays. This package implements Monday/Wednesday/Friday/Sunday (matching the SI Appendix's dedicated SMS-survey description), 8 occurrences per 2-week phase, consistent with all four citations on the shared fact that there are exactly 4 SMS prompts/week.
fields.derivation: Implementation choice made to resolve a verbatim weekday conflict across the source documents; the 4x/week cadence and 8-occurrences-per-phase count are not in dispute.

nodes.summary: Overall experimental design: 2-arm crossover waitlist-control RCT with 3 measurement waves.

nodes.title: Prolific-recruited iPhone users (N=467 randomized)

fields.label: Recruitment & eligibility
fields.value: American and Canadian participants recruited from Prolific.co; only iPhone users were eligible (for compatibility with the Freedom blocking app).

fields.label: Randomized sample size
fields.value: 504 complete baseline responses; 253 randomized to Intervention, 251 to Delayed Intervention; after deduplication, 467 unique participants retained (242 Intervention, 225 Delayed Intervention).

fields.label: Demographics
fields.value: Average age 32; 63% female; education: 20% high school only, 11% some community college, 37% undergraduate degree, 8% master's, 3% doctorate; race/ethnicity: 15% Asian, 9% Black, 62% White, 12% Other; employment: 29% students, 42% full-time employed, 16% part-time employed.

fields.label: Compensation
fields.value: $5 USD for the baseline survey; Canadian participants $50 CAD (survey 2) and $45 CAD (survey 3); American participants a $40 USD and then $35 USD Amazon.com gift card. Same amounts/timing regardless of condition; payment was explicitly not contingent on compliance.

fields.label: Ethics approval & consent
fields.value: Approved by the University of British Columbia Institutional Review Board; all participants gave informed consent (verbatim consent-form text was not reproduced in the paper or SI Appendix).

nodes.summary: Who took part, how they were recruited, and how they were paid.

nodes.title: Four-week study timeline

fields.label: Timeline
fields.value: Baseline survey (T1) -> random assignment -> Phase 1 (weeks 1-2): Intervention blocks mobile internet, Delayed Intervention continues normal use, both receive 8 SMS mood/time-use prompts -> T2 survey (+2 weeks) -> Phase 2 (weeks 3-4): roles swap (Intervention regains access, Delayed Intervention now blocks), both receive 8 more SMS prompts -> T3 survey (+4 weeks).
fields.derivation: Assembled from the design, compliance, and experience-sampling sections of the Results and Materials and methods.

nodes.summary: Narrative summary of the full four-week procedure; operationalized step-by-step below.

nodes.title: Freedom-app blocking instructions (reported)

fields.label: Instructions given to the Intervention group
fields.value: You are given a code to download the premium version of the Freedom app, which can block all mobile internet (Wi-Fi and mobile data), together with detailed instructions for installing it and setting up a complete mobile internet block that will last 2 weeks. The app offers a 'Locked Mode' that makes it impossible to disable the block from within the app once set.

fields.label: Instructions given to the Delayed Intervention group
fields.value: You are informed that your mobile internet block will begin 2 weeks later; during the first 2 weeks you continue using your phone normally.

fields.label: Payment independence disclosure given to participants
fields.value: At T2 and T3 participants were told they were eligible to 'receive compensation even if you did not manage to keep the Internet blocked from your phone for the entire 2 weeks.'

nodes.title: Condition × Time effect on SMS mood (phase 1 and phase 2)

fields.label: Result kind
fields.value: both reported (published) and new_observation (executable at run time)

fields.label: Contrast
fields.value: Within each phase: condition main effect on mean mood; condition × time (1-8) interaction on mood slope, via multilevel model in the paper (this package uses an OLS approximation, see evaluation.py)
fields.derivation: Paper used REML multilevel models with Satterthwaite df; this package's evaluate() approximates the same contrasts with ordinary least squares on session-level data because a full mixed-model fit is out of scope for a dependency-free evaluator.

fields.label: Reported statistics (published finding)
fields.value: Phase 1: Intervention M=6.62 (SE .13) vs Delayed M=6.02 (SE .13), b=0.59, P=.001; Intervention mood slope b=0.05, P=.045; Delayed slope b=-0.02, P=.501. Phase 2: Condition×Time interaction b=-0.09, P=.001; Delayed (now blocked) slope b=0.08, P<.001; Intervention (now free) slope b=-0.02, P=.423.

fields.label: Can this package currently execute this analysis on fresh agent sessions?
fields.derivation: mat_sms_mood is verbatim and fully specified, so run_sessions can collect real SMS-mood trajectories and evaluate() can compute the matching contrasts.

steps.title: Random assignment to Intervention or Delayed Intervention

rule.label: Randomization rule
rule.value: Participants are randomly assigned to Intervention or Delayed Intervention at roughly a 1:1 ratio (observed: 253 vs. 251 at baseline; 242 vs. 225 in the final retained sample).

steps.title: Intervention arm: install Freedom app and block mobile internet

rule.label: Compliance-modeling choice
rule.value: This package does not sample a fixed compliance probability from the paper's observed 25.5% compliance rate. Each agent decides for itself, in character, whether/when to disable the block; compliance is an emergent property of the run, not a preset input. This matches the fidelity rule against replacing a participant with a sampled distribution, but means a given run's compliance rate is not guaranteed to match the published 25.5%.

evidence.quote: We conducted a month-long randomized controlled trial to investigate how removing constant access to the internet through smartphones might impact psychological functioning. We used a mobile phone application to block all mobile internet access from participants' smartphones for 2 weeks and objectively track compliance.

We report such an experiment, finding that blocking mobile internet for 2 weeks reduces smartphone use and improves subjective well-being (SWB) (including life satisfaction and positive affect), mental health (more than antidepressants), and sustained attention (as much as being 10 years younger).

We preregistered three key outcomes. First, we measured SWB using the standard tripartite model that consists of self-reported positive affect, negative affect, and life satisfaction (21). Second, we assessed overall mental health by measuring a range of mental health outcomes, such as symptoms of anxiety and depression, using diagnostic tools developed by the American Psychiatric Association (22). Finally, we examined attentional functioning using both self-reported attentional awareness (23) and objectively measured sustained attention.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: those in the Intervention group blocked mobile internet access for the first 2 weeks only (T1–T2), while those in the Delayed Intervention group acted as a control for the first 2 weeks and then blocked mobile internet access for the second 2 weeks (T2–T3). This cross-over design let us test whether any effects persist post intervention and increased power by administering the intervention to all participants, albeit at different times.
We intentionally chose a waitlist control, as our primary goal is to examine the effect of the status quo (constant access to mobile internet).
119 (25.5% of those who committed) met our preregistered definition of “compliant” (having the block active for at least 10 of the 14 intervention days, as recorded by the Freedom app).
Of these 249, 119 were deemed “compliant” based on our preregistered criteria of disabling the internet block fewer than five times during the intervention period.
We asked participants to upload screenshots of their iPhone's screen time page showing their average daily screen time in the past week.

We recruited American and Canadian participants from Prolific.co, an online labor pool. Only iPhone users were eligible to participate due to compatibility with the Freedom app that we used to block mobile internet. The average age was 32 years; 63% were female; 20% had only a high school diploma; 11% had attended community college; 37% had an undergraduate degree; 8% had a master's degree; and 3% had a doctorate. Fifteen percent of participants identify as Asian, 9% as Black, 62% as White, and 12% as Other. Twenty-nine percent were students, 42% were employed full-time, and 16% were employed part-time.

All participants were paid $5 USD for the baseline survey. Canadian participants were paid $50 Canadian dollars for the second survey and $45 for the third, while American participants were sent a $40 USD Amazon.com gift card for the second survey and a $35 USD Amazon.com gift card for the third.
This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of British Columbia. All participants gave informed consent.

We received 504 complete responses to the baseline survey, with 253 randomly assigned to the Intervention group and 251 to the Delayed Intervention group. After removing duplicate email addresses, phone numbers, and Prolific IDs, we retained 467 unique participants (242 in Intervention and 225 in Delayed Intervention; see CONSORT diagram in Fig. 3 for details of how the sample size changed over the course of the experiment due to attrition and invalid responses).

Participants who were assigned to the Intervention group were given a code to download the premium version of the Freedom app and detailed instructions for how to install it and set up a complete mobile internet block that would last for 2 weeks; those assigned to the Delayed Intervention group were informed that their mobile internet block would begin 2 weeks later.

free copy of the premium Freedom app that can block all mobile internet and use a “Locked Mode” that makes it impossible to disable the block from within the app. Redeeming this code to sign up for an account on the Freedom app was therefore required to begin blocking mobile internet.

Surveys 2 and 3 were only available for 48 h after we sent them to participants, in order to decrease the likelihood that the intervention's effects might have “worn off” before we could measure them.

We supplemented this main survey with brief SMS surveys measuring mood and time use, sent to participants every Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday during the 4 weeks of the experiment.
We used text messages (SMS) to briefly assess mood and behavior during the study. Participants received four text messages per week on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays.
we created a variable, Time, that indicated the survey number in order from 1 to 8 for each of the two study phases (phase 1: first 2 weeks; phase 2: second 2 weeks).
The mood question was “How do you feel right now on a scale from 1 (bad) to 10 (good)?” and participants simply replied to the text message with a number between 1 and 10.

evidence.quote: The time use question was “Which of the following did you do yesterday? Please text back the corresponding number(s) in a single text (e.g. 1 2 3).” 1. Socialized in person 2. Socialized via phone or video call 3. Communicated via text message 4. Exercised 5. Pursued a hobby 6. Slept enough to feel fully rested
we sent participants brief SMS text message surveys every Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday during the four weeks of the experiment.
We explored time use by asking participants whether they had spent more or less time than they normally do on a range of online and offline activities (from 1—a lot less to 5—a lot more).
We measured the potential mediator of time use using self-reports of time spent on ten different activities during the past week, relative to what is typical.

Table S4. Factor loadings for time use questions. Item / Factor 1 / Factor 2 / Factor 3 ... Exercising .772; Pursuing hobbies .736; Time in nature .700; Time with friends/family in person .600; Reading a book .431; Communicating with friends/family via voice/video .880; Communicating with friends/family via text .847; Watching YouTube .793; Reading the news .662; Watching TV or movies .652

these activities loaded on three factors, which we call “time in the offline world” (socializing in person, exercising, being in nature, pursuing a hobby, and reading a book), “digital communication” (communicating via text message, voice, or video calls on any device), and “media consumption” (reading the news, watching TV or movies, and watching YouTube on any device).
We assessed sleep by asking people how many hours they had slept per night, on average, during the past week.

we asked how motivated participants were to reduce their smartphone use on a 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much) scale and 83% of our participants chose 5 or higher. Seventy-nine percent also felt highly capable of reducing their smartphone use.

SWB was measured using the tripartite model (45), which consists of life satisfaction, measured using the Satisfaction with Life Scale (21), and positive and negative affect, measured using the Scale of Positive and Negative Experience (46). These measures were averaged to create a SWB index (α = 0.82).

The mental health measures were created by the American Psychiatric Association (22) and included brief measures of depression, anxiety, anger, social anxiety, and personality functioning. Contrary to preregistration, we did not measure repetitive thoughts and behaviors. Items were taken from the corresponding subscales of the DSM-5 Level 1 cross-cutting symptom measure for adults. We also selected an additional item to measure social anxiety from the severity measure for social anxiety disorder. We combined these into a single index of mental health (α = 0.90).

Attentional awareness (a self-reported measure of attentional functioning) was measured using the six-item Attentional Lapses subscale of the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (α = 0.93) (45), which assesses the tendency “run on automatic” and have difficulty focusing on the present moment.
we measured social connectedness with the validated three-item Relatedness Scale (47), α = 0.93
self-control with an abbreviated six-item version of the self-control scale (38), α = 0.82
we measured participants' baseline FoMO, with an abbreviated six-item version of the 10-item FoMO Scale (40), α = 0.83

we measured self-reported attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder symptoms at baseline using a validated six-item version of the World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale, α = 0.81 (48).

Immediately following the surveys, participants were redirected to a 5 min online version of the gradCPT task, which we used to objectively measure sustained attention. The gradCPT (24, 27) is a well-validated and widely used go/no-go continuous performance task (27, 49) in which participants are asked to react by pressing a button on the keyboard (space bar) when cities are shown (90% of trials), but not when mountains are shown (10% of trials). Using standard signal detection analyses, errors (commission, or presses to mountains; omission, nonresponses to cities) are used to calculate d-prime, a measure of discrimination ability and the key measure of sustained attention provided by gradCPT.

After 2 weeks of blocking mobile internet (T1–T2), the Intervention group displayed significant improvements from baseline in SWB (an index including life satisfaction and positive and negative affect; dz = 0.46, P < 0.001), mental health (a reverse-scored index including symptoms of depression, anxiety, anger, personality function, and social anxiety; dz = 0.57, P < 0.001), and objectively measured sustained attention ability (defined as task accuracy, or d-prime score, on the gradCPT; dz = 0.24, P = 0.008).
ANOVA revealed an effect of Time, F(2,576) = 22.13, P < 0.001, Condition, F(1,302) = 3.52, P = 0.062, and their interaction, F(2,576) = 12.94, P < 0.001.

We found that participants in the Intervention condition had higher mood on average (M = 6.62, SE = 0.13) than participants in the Delayed Intervention condition (M = 6.02, SE = 0.13) during the initial 2-week phase of the study (b = 0.59, P = 0.001, d = 0.33; see Table S1, Model S1). We also found that participants in the Intervention group felt progressively better over the first 2 weeks as indicated by a positive slope across the eight consecutive measurements between T1 and T2, b = 0.05, P = 0.045. Participants in the Delayed Intervention did not show significant improvements in mood over the first 2 weeks, b = −0.02, P = 0.501.

We found a significant Time*Condition interaction, b = −0.09, t(225) = −3.23, P = 0.001. Simple effects analyses indicated a significant improvement in mood within Delayed Intervention participants (i.e. those currently undergoing Intervention), b = 0.08, t(235) = 3.65, P < 0.001, and no change in mood in the Intervention participants, b = −0.02, t(230) = −.80, P = 0.423.

blocking mobile internet increased time spent in the offline world (dz = 0.70, P < 0.001) and decreased time spent consuming media (dz = 0.41, P < 0.001). The intervention did not affect time spent on digital communication through talk and text, which were not blocked by our intervention (dz = 0.08, P = 0.163).

the intervention increased time spent in the “offline world” (Mpre = 2.75, SD = 0.63; Mpost = 3.36, SD = 0.66; F(1,311) = 150.610, P < 0.001, dz = 0.70) and decreased time spent consuming media (Mpre = 3.10, SD = 0.67; Mpost = 2.70, SD = 0.79; F(1,311) = 53.138, P < 0.001, dz = −0.42).

Across both conditions, 70.5% of participants reported better mental health postintervention than preintervention; this figure was 73.3% for SWB and 58.5% for objectively measured sustained attention. Overall, 90.7% of participants experienced an improvement in at least one of these three outcomes.

individual differences in baseline FoMO significantly moderated the effect of the mobile internet block on SWB (F(1,304) = 8.330, P = 0.004) and mental health (F(1,304) = 12.434, P < 0.001)... individual differences in baseline ADHD significantly moderated the effect of the mobile internet block on attentional awareness (F(1,305) = 22.006, P < 0.001)

For SWB, the total effect of the intervention (c = 0.424, 95% CI [0.31, 0.53]) was mediated by indirect effects of increased time spent in the offline world (a1b1 = 0.072, 95% CI [0.00, 0.15]), decreased time spent consuming media (a2b2 = 0.046, 95% CI [0.01, 0.10]), heightened feelings of social connectedness (a3b3 = 0.084, 95% CI [0.05, 0.14]), improved self-control (a4b4 = 0.169, 95% CI [0.10, 0.26]), and increased sleep (a5b5 = 0.020, 95% CI [0.00, 0.10]).
For sustained attention, the total effect of the intervention on gradCPT performance (c = 0.159, 95% CI [0.07, 0.25]) was not significantly mediated by any of the factors included in our analysis.

issues.reason: The paper and SI Appendix cite the instrument/task but do not print its item-level wording (or, for gradCPT and the screen-time screenshot, the measure requires a real device/visual reaction-time task that a text-only LLM participant cannot perform). issues.title: SMS cadence weekday conflict (phase 1): Sunday (p.6, SI) vs. Saturday (p.7)
issues.reason: Page 6 and the SI Appendix state the SMS surveys were sent every Monday/Wednesday/Friday/Sunday; page 7 states Mondays/Wednesdays/Fridays/Saturdays. Both describe the same 4x/week cadence but disagree on the fourth weekday.
issues.impact: Changes which calendar day the 4th weekly SMS prompt lands on; does not change the total count (8 per phase) or the mood/time-use item content.
issues.suggestedAction: Researcher should confirm the intended weekday from the OSF preregistration/materials (not fetched here) and update step_phase1_sms_loop.rule if Saturday is correct.

issues.suggestedAction: Resolve together with issue_sms_cadence_phase1 from the OSF preregistration/materials.

issues.title: Compliance with the mobile-internet block is emergent, not sampled
issues.reason: The paper reports an empirically observed compliance rate (25.5%) but gives no algorithmic rule for deciding, in advance, which participants comply. Per the fidelity rules, this package does not sample from that published rate; each agent participant decides in character.
issues.impact: A given run's compliance rate is a genuine model output, not guaranteed to match 25.5%; this is intentional and should not be 'fixed' by injecting the paper's statistic as an input.
issues.suggestedAction: No action required; documented for transparency. If a researcher specifically wants to study TOT-matched behavior, they can post-filter sessions by each session's own self-reported compliance log.
